english: Why do you harass undeserving strangers, dog,
note: hospites: strangers, passers-by (literally guests).

english: cowardly against wolves?
note: ignavos = ignavus, agreeing with canis (line 1).

latin: quin huc inanis, si potes, vertis minas
english: why not turn here, if you can, your empty threats
note: quin with the indicative: 'why do you not'; 'your' supplied; inanis = inanes, with minas.

english: and go for me, who will bite back?
note: remorsurum: future participle, 'about to bite back'.

latin: nam qualis aut Molossus aut fulvos Lacon,
english: For like either a Molossian or a tawny Laconian,
note: Molossian and Laconian (Spartan) hounds; fulvos = fulvus.

english: a friendly force to shepherds,
note: vis: the dog as a strength friendly to shepherds.

latin: agam per altas aure sublata nivis
english: I shall drive through the deep, with ear raised, snows
note: altas agrees with nivis (= nives, accusative plural); agam is future.

english: whatever wild beast shall go ahead;
note: praecedet: future.

latin: tu, cum timenda voce complesti nemus,
english: you, when with a voice to be feared you have filled the grove,
note: complesti = complevisti.

english: sniff at the food thrown out.
note: proiectum cibum: food thrown to the dog, as by a thief, to quiet it.

latin: cave, cave, namque in malos asperrimus
english: Beware, beware, for against the wicked, most fierce,
note: asperrimus describes the speaker.

english: I raise ready horns,
note: Metaphor: the speaker as a bull ready to gore; meaning, ready with attacking verse.

english: like the son-in-law spurned by faithless Lycambes
note: Archilochus, rejected as son-in-law by Lycambes, attacked him in iambics; Lycambae is dative of the agent.

english: or the keen enemy to Bupalus.
note: Hipponax, who lampooned the sculptor Bupalus.

latin: an si quis atro dente me petiverit,
english: Or if anyone with black tooth shall have gone for me,
note: petiverit: future perfect; 'black tooth': malicious, envious slander.

english: unavenged, like a boy, shall I weep?
note: ut: 'like'; flebo is future.

latin: Quo, quo scelesti ruitis? aut cur dexteris
english: Where, where, wicked ones, are you rushing? Or why to right hands
note: dexteris goes with aptantur (line 2).

english: are swords fitted, that were sheathed?
note: conditi: put away, sheathed (after the earlier civil wars).

english: Too little, is it, over the plains and Neptune
note: Neptune: the sea (metonymy); super governs campis and Neptuno.

english: has been poured of Latin blood,
note: parum ... sanguinis (line 3): 'too little of Latin blood'.

english: not so that the proud of envious Carthage
note: superbas agrees with arces (line 6).

english: the Roman might burn citadels,
note: arces with superbas (line 5); ureret: subjunctive of purpose.

english: or the untouched Briton so that he might go down
note: intactus: not yet conquered; descenderet: subjunctive of purpose.

english: the Sacred, chained, Way,
note: sacra ... via: 'by the Sacred Way', the route of a triumph, where captives walked in chains.

latin: sed ut Secundum vota Parthorum sua
english: but so that, according to the Parthians' prayers, by its own
note: sua agrees with dextera (line 10); Secundum (preposition 'according to') is capitalized in the source.

english: this City should perish, right hand?
note: dextera with sua (line 9): 'by its own right hand'; periret: subjunctive of purpose.

latin: neque hic lupis mos nec fuit leonibus
english: Neither this for wolves the custom, nor has it been for lions,
note: fuit serves both clauses

english: ever, except against an unlike kind, being fierce.
note: feris: adjective 'fierce', agreeing with lupis and leonibus (line 11); they are fierce only toward a different kind.

latin: furorne caecos an rapit vis acrior
english: Does frenzy sweep you blind, or a keener force,
note: caecos: accusative, you (Romans) blind

english: or guilt? Give an answer.

latin: tacent et albus ora pallor inficit
english: They are silent, and a white pallor stains their faces
note: 'their' supplied; ora: plural, faces.

english: and their minds, struck, are stunned.
note: 'their' supplied; Stupent is capitalized in the source.

latin: sic est: acerba fata Romanos agunt
english: So it is: bitter fates drive the Romans
and the crime of a brother's slaying,
note: fraternae necis: literally 'of fraternal killing'.

latin: ut inmerentis fluxit in terram Remi
english: since there flowed onto the earth undeserving Remus'
note: Remi goes with cruor (line 20); ut: 'from the time when'.

english: blood, a curse to his descendants.
note: sacer: accursed, bringing a curse upon; 'his' supplied.

english: To think that you ask, rotten with long age,
note: Exclamatory infinitive: 'that you should ask!'

english: what unsinews my powers,
note: enervet: unsinews, unmans; the pun with nervi (8.17)

latin: cum sit tibi dens ater et rugis vetus
english: when you have a black tooth, and, old, with wrinkles
note: Literally 'there is to you a black tooth'; vetus agrees with senectus (line 4).

english: age should plough your forehead,
note: 'your' supplied; exaret: metaphor, furrows with wrinkles; subjunctive in the cum clause.

english: and should gape, foul, between dried-up buttocks,
note: hiet: subjunctive in the cum clause, like exaret (8.4)

english: an anus like [that] of a costive cow.
note: podex: anus; crudae: with undigested food, costive.

latin: sed incitat me pectus et mammae putres
english: But the chest arouses me, and the rotten breasts
note: Ironic; putres: crumbling, flabby.

english: such as a mare's udders,
note: equina: adjective, 'of a mare'.

english: and the soft belly, and a thigh, onto swollen
note: tumentibus agrees with suris (line 10).

english: thin, calves added.
note: femur exile ... tumentibus suris additum (lines 9-10): 'a thin thigh set on swollen calves'.

english: Be rich, and the funeral may ancestral masks
note: esto: 'granted, be'; imagines: wax masks of ancestors carried in a funeral; funus is the object of ducant (line 12).

english: lead, triumphal ones, yours,
note: tuom = tuum, agreeing with funus (line 11); triumphales: of ancestors who held triumphs.

english: and may there be no wife who, with rounder
note: rotundioribus agrees with bacis (line 14).

english: loaded berries, would walk about.
note: bacis: literally 'berries', i.e. pearls (metaphor); onusta: laden.

latin: quid? quod libelli Stoici inter Sericos
english: What? Because little Stoic books among silken
note: Sericos agrees with pulvillos (line 16); Seres: the Chinese, source of silk.

english: cushions love to lie,
are unlettered sinews any less stiff
note: num expects the answer no; nervi: sinews, i.e. the penis.

english: or does the phallus droop less?
note: fascinum: the penis (originally the phallic amulet).

latin: quod ut superbo provoces ab inguine,
english: And to call it up from a haughty groin
note: quod: 'which' (the fascinum); provoces: subjunctive of purpose, rouse; superbo: disdainful.

english: with your mouth you must labour.
note: 'your' supplied; adlaborandum est tibi: gerundive of obligation; oral stimulation is meant.

latin: Quando repositum Caecubum ad festas dapes
english: When the stored Caecuban, for festal feasts,
note: Caecubum: Caecuban wine, the object of bibam (line 4).

english: glad with Caesar victor,
note: victore ... Caesare: ablative absolute, 'Caesar being victor'.

english: with you beneath the lofty—so it pleases Jove—house,
note: alta agrees with domo; Maecenas's house on the Esquiline; Iovi: Jove.

english: blessed Maecenas, shall I drink,
note: bibam: future (or deliberative subjunctive).

english: with the lyre sounding a song mixed with pipes,
note: sonante ... lyra: ablative absolute; tibiis: reed-pipes.

english: this one Dorian, those barbarian?
note: hac: the lyre; illis: the pipes; barbarian: the Phrygian mode.

latin: ut nuper, actus cum freto Neptunius
english: as lately, when, driven from the strait, the Neptunian
note: Neptunius agrees with dux (line 8): Sextus Pompey, who styled himself son of Neptune; the strait: of Sicily.

english: leader fled, his ships burnt,
note: 'his' supplied; ustis navibus: ablative absolute (Naulochus, 36 BC).

english: having threatened the City with chains which he had taken off
slaves, a friend to the treacherous ones.
note: servis goes with detraxerat (line 9) and with perfidis: he was friend to the treacherous slaves whose chains he removed.

english: A Roman, alas—you, posterity, will deny it—
note: 'it' supplied; posteri: those born later.

english: made over as property to a woman,
note: emancipatus: legal transfer to another's ownership; the woman is Cleopatra.

latin: fert vallum et arma miles et spadonibus
english: carries stake and arms as a soldier, and to eunuchs
note: vallum: palisade stakes carried by Roman soldiers; miles is in apposition to Romanus (line 11).

english: wrinkled, he can be a slave,
note: rugosis agrees with spadonibus (line 13).

english: and among the standards, a shameful, military,
note: turpe agrees with conopium (line 16); militaria with signa.

english: the sun looks upon mosquito-net.
note: conopium: a mosquito-net canopy, an Egyptian luxury.

latin: ad hunc frementis verterunt bis mille equos
english: At this, snorting, they turned two thousand horses,
note: frementis = frementes, with equos; ad hunc: at this sight (or toward him, Caesar).

english: the Gauls, chanting Caesar,
note: Galli: the Galatians, who deserted Antony.

english: and of the enemy's ships, in harbour lie hidden
note: hostilium agrees with navium.

english: the sterns, leftward set in motion.
note: puppes: ships; sinistrorsum citae: obscure, perhaps 'backing to port' or retreating.

english: Io Triumph, do you delay the golden
note: Triumphus addressed as a god; aureos agrees with currus (line 22).

english: chariots and the untouched heifers?
note: intactas: never yoked, as sacrificial victims must be.

english: Io Triumph, neither from the Jugurthine an equal
note: Iugurthino agrees with bello, parem with ducem (line 24).

english: war have you brought back a leader
note: Marius, victor over Jugurtha.

english: nor Africanus, for whom over Carthage
note: Scipio, conqueror of Carthage.

english: valour founded a tomb.
note: Sepulcrum (capitalized in the source): his monument of glory raised on the ruins of Carthage.

english: On land and sea conquered, the enemy for a purple
note: Punico (with sago understood): the scarlet general's cloak.

english: mourning has exchanged cloak.
note: lugubre agrees with sagum: Antony has put on a soldier's mourning cloak in place of the general's scarlet.

latin: aut ille centum nobilem Cretam urbibus
english: Either he Crete, famous for its hundred cities,
note: 'its' supplied; Cretam is the object of petit (line 31).

english: about to go with winds not his own,
note: 'his' supplied: unfavourable winds.

english: is making for, or the Syrtes worked by the south wind,
note: exercitatas agrees with Syrtis (= Syrtes, the African sandbanks); noto: the south wind.

english: or he is carried on an uncertain sea.
Bring here, boy, larger cups
note: capaciores: more capacious; Scyphos (capitalized in the source): drinking cups.

english: and Chian wines or Lesbian,
or what would check the flowing nausea,
note: quod: the Caecuban (line 36); coerceat: subjunctive.

english: measure out for us, Caecuban.
Care and fear for Caesar's affairs it is pleasing
note: Caesaris rerum: 'for Caesar's fortunes'.

english: with sweet Lyaeus to loosen.
note: Lyaeus: 'the Loosener', Bacchus, i.e. wine.

english: Under an evil bird, released, the ship goes out,
note: mala ... alite: with an evil omen (alite: bird of omen); soluta: loosed from its moorings.

english: carrying stinking Mevius.
note: Mevius: a poetaster.

english: That with bristling you may lash both its sides,
note: horridis agrees with fluctibus (line 4); 'its' supplied.

english: Auster, remember, waves;
note: fluctibus with horridis (line 3); Auster: the south wind.

english: let black Eurus the ropes, on the overturned sea,
note: rudentis = rudentes, the object of differat (line 6); Eurus: the east wind.

english: and the broken oars, scatter;
note: differat: subjunctive of wish.

english: let Aquilo rise, as great as when on high mountains
note: Aquilo: the north wind.

english: he breaks trembling holm-oaks;
note: ilics = ilices; trementis = trementes.

latin: nec sidus atra nocte amicum adpareat,
english: nor let a friendly star in black night appear,
where gloomy Orion sets;
note: Orion's setting brought storms.

english: nor let it be borne on a calmer sea
note: quietiore agrees with aequore.

english: than the Greek band of victors,

latin: cum Pallas usto vertit iram ab Ilio
english: when Pallas turned from burnt Ilium her anger
note: 'her' supplied.

english: onto the impious ship of Ajax.
note: Ajax son of Oileus, who violated Cassandra in Athena's temple.

latin: o quantus instat navitis sudor tuis
english: O how much sweat presses upon your sailors
note: quantus agrees with sudor.

english: and on you a yellow pallor
and that unmanly wailing
note: non virilis: 'not manly'.

english: and prayers to Jove turned away,
note: aversum: turned away from you, deaf to your prayers.

english: when the Ionian, bellowing back with a wet
note: udo agrees with Noto (line 20); sinus: the Ionian gulf.

english: south wind, shall have broken the keel!
note: ruperit: future perfect; Notus: the south wind.

english: But if, a rich prize, on the curving shore
note: opima agrees with praeda; curvo with litore.

english: stretched out, shall have delighted the sea-birds,
note: iuverit: third person, its subject praeda (10.21)

english: a lustful he-goat will be sacrificed
and a lamb to the Storms.
note: Tempestates: storm goddesses.

latin: Petti, nihil me sicut antea iuvat
english: Pettius, not at all does it please me, as before,
note: Petti: vocative of Pettius.

english: to write little verses, struck by heavy love,

latin: amore, qui me praeter omnis expetit
english: by love, which seeks me out beyond all others
note: omnis = omnes.

latin: mollibus in pueris aut in puellis urere.
english: for soft boys or for girls to burn.
note: urere: to set (me) on fire with love for.

latin: hic tertius December, ex quo destiti
english: This third December, since I ceased
note: hic tertius December: 'this is the third December'.

english: to rage for Inachia, from the woods their glory shakes.
note: 'their' supplied; honorem: foliage (metaphor, the woods' glory).

latin: heu me, per Vrbem (nam pudet tanti mali)
english: Ah me, through the City (for I am ashamed of so great an ill)
note: pudet: impersonal, 'it shames (me)'.

latin: fabula quanta fui, conviviorum et paenitet,
english: what a great story I was! I regret the banquets too,
note: fabula: gossip, talk of the town; paenitet: impersonal.

latin: in quis amantem languor et silentium
english: in which, as a lover, listlessness and silence
note: quis = quibus; amantem: 'me, a lover', object of arguit.

latin: arguit et latere petitus imo spiritus.
english: proved me, and breath sought from the lowest side.
note: 'me' supplied; arguit: exposed, convicted; a sigh fetched from deep in the chest.

english: “That against gain nothing avails the candid
note: candidum agrees with ingenium (line 12).

english: talent of a poor man!” I complained, weeping to you,
note: ingenium: native talent, character.

english: as soon as, of me heated, the shameless god
note: calentis: genitive, 'of one warm (with wine)', with arcana (line 14); deus: Bacchus.

english: with more fiery neat wine had moved the secrets from their place.
note: promorat = promoverat; mero: unmixed wine; 'their' supplied.

english: “But if in my breast there should boil
note: praecordia: the chest, seat of feeling.

latin: libera bilis, ut haec ingrata ventis dividat
english: free bile, so that these thankless it would scatter to the winds,
note: haec ingrata agrees with fomenta (line 17); bilis: bile, anger.

english: salves, in no way relieving the evil wound,
note: fomenta: poultices; metaphor for consolations.

english: shame will cease, set aside, to contend with unequals.”
note: pudor ... desinet: shame removed, he will stop competing with unworthy rivals.

latin: ubi haec severus te palam laudaveram,
english: When, stern, I had praised these things openly to you,
note: te palam: in your presence.

latin: iussus abire domum ferebar incerto pede
english: bidden to go home, I was carried with uncertain foot

latin: ad non amicos heu mihi postis et heu
english: to the not friendly, alas for me, doorposts and, alas,
note: postis = postes; non amicos: unfriendly, the beloved's door.

latin: limina dura, quibus lumbos et infregi latus.
english: hard thresholds, on which I broke both my loins and my side.
note: 'my' supplied.

english: Now of one boasting that any little woman
note: gloriantis agrees with Lycisci (line 24).

latin: vincere mollitia amor Lycisci me tenet;
english: he surpasses in softness, love of Lyciscus holds me;
note: vincere: infinitive dependent on gloriantis (line 23); Lycisci: love for Lyciscus.

english: from which could set me free not friends'
note: 'me' supplied; amicorum goes with consilia (line 26).

english: frank counsels, nor grave insults,
note: libera: outspoken.

latin: sed alius ardor aut puellae candidae
english: but another passion, either for a fair girl

latin: aut teretis pueri longam renodantis comam.
english: or for a smooth boy, tying back his long hair.
note: 'his' supplied; renodantis: tying back (some take it as 'untying').

latin: Quid tibi vis, mulier nigris dignissima barris?
english: What do you want for yourself, woman most worthy of black elephants?
note: barris: elephants (a rare word).

english: Why gifts to me, why notes
note: tabellas: writing-tablets, love-letters.

latin: mittis nec firmo iuveni neque naris obesae?
english: do you send, a young man not vigorous and not of a dull nose?
note: nec firmo: not sexually vigorous; naris obesae: literally 'of a fat nostril', blunt of smell.

english: For more keenly, uniquely, I smell out
note: unus: 'I alone'.

latin: polypus an gravis hirsutis cubet hircus in alis
english: whether a polyp or a heavy goat lies in hairy armpits
note: polypus: a nasal polyp, stinking; hircus: he-goat, the goatish smell of the armpits.

latin: quam canis acer ubi lateat sus.
english: than a keen dog where a pig may hide.
note: sus: pig or boar.

latin: qui sudor vietis et quam malus undique membris
english: What sweat, and how bad, everywhere from shrivelled limbs,
note: vietis agrees with membris.

english: rises a smell, when, with penis limp,
note: pene soluto: ablative absolute, the speaker's penis limp; Soluto is capitalized in the source.

latin: indomitam properat rabiem sedare, neque illi
english: her untamed frenzy she hurries to allay, and no longer on her
note: 'her' supplied (with rabiem); illi: dative, 'for her'.

english: does the moist chalk stay, and the colour
note: creta: chalk cosmetic.

english: painted with crocodile's dung; and now, in heat,
note: stercore crocodili: crocodile dung used as a face cosmetic; Subando (capitalized in the source): being in heat, used of animals.

english: she bursts the taut bed and canopy.
note: tenta cubilia: the bed-frame with tight cords; tecta: canopy; both plural in the Latin.

latin: vel mea cum saevis agitat fastidia verbis:
english: Or when with savage words she assails my disgust:
note: fastidia: squeamishness, distaste.

english: “With Inachia you are limp less than with me;
note: langues: you are limp, impotent.

latin: Inachiam ter nocte potes, mihi Semper ad unum
english: Inachia three times a night you can, for me always for one
note: potes: you are able (sexually); Semper is capitalized in the source.

latin: mollis opus. pereat male quae te
english: job soft. May she perish miserably who, to you
note: mollis: limp, agreeing with 'you'; te goes with quaerenti (line 17).

english: Lesbia, seeking a bull, showed an impotent one.
note: Lesbia: a go-between who recommended him; taurum: a bull, a virile lover; inertem: sluggish, impotent.

english: when for me Coan Amyntas was at hand,
note: Cous: of Cos.

latin: cuius in indomito constantior inguine nervos
english: in whose untamed groin a more steadfast sinew
note: nervos (= nervus): sinew, the penis

english: than a young tree on the hills is fixed.
With Tyrian purple-shells redyed fleeces of wool
note: muricibus: murex shellfish, source of purple dye; iteratae: dipped twice.

english: for whom were they hurried? For you, surely,

latin: ne foret aequalis inter conviva, magis quem
english: so that there should not be among your peers a guest whom more
note: 'your' supplied; inter follows aequalis (= aequales); conviva: guest at a banquet.

english: his woman should love than you.
note: sua: 'his own'.

latin: o ego non felix, quam tu fugis, ut pavet acris
english: O I, unhappy, whom you flee, as dreads the fierce
note: acris = acres, agreeing with lupos (line 26); non felix: 'not fortunate'.

english: lamb wolves, and she-goats lions!”
note: capreae: roe-deer or wild she-goats.
